title: Historical Background and What Is Formalized
content: The module docstring surveys 175 years of failed attempts: de Polignac's 1849 conjecture, Brun's 1919 convergence of the reciprocal sum, Hardy-Littlewood's 1923 quantitative prediction, and the 2014–2015 Zhang-Maynard bounded-gaps breakthrough (gap ≤ 246). The file then states exactly what it contributes: 25 verified pairs, two equivalent reformulations of TPC, and three conditional consequences. The `open TwinPrimes` imports `IsTwinPrimePair`, `TwinPrimeConjecture`, the `twin_prime_conjecture` axiom, and the `twin_prime_mod_six` structure theorem from the parent file.
mathContext: Key imports from parent: `IsTwinPrimePair p := Prime(p) ∧ Prime(p+2)`, `TwinPrimeConjecture := ∀ N, ∃ p > N, IsTwinPrimePair p`, and `axiom twin_prime_conjecture : TwinPrimeConjecture`. The structure theorem states: $p > 3 \Rightarrow (\text{IsTwinPrimePair}(p) \Leftrightarrow p \equiv 5 \pmod{6})$.

title: 19 New Certified Twin Prime Pairs via `decide`
content: The 19 theorems (`twin_59` through `twin_521`) each have the proof `by constructor <;> decide`. The `constructor` splits `IsTwinPrimePair p = Prime(p) ∧ Prime(p+2)` into two goals; `decide` closes both by running Lean's kernel primality check for each concrete number. The closing theorem `exists_twentyfive_twin_primes` packages all 25 pairs (6 from parent + 19 new) into a single conjunction proved by an anonymous term-mode constructor.
mathContext: New lower elements: $\{59, 71, 101, 107, 137, 149, 179, 191, 197, 227, 239, 269, 281, 311, 347, 419, 431, 461, 521\}$. Every element satisfies $p \equiv 5 \pmod{6}$ (since $p > 3$), consistent with the structure theorem from the parent. The corresponding twin pairs are $(59,61), (71,73), \ldots, (521, 523)$.

title: TPC ↔ No Finite Bound: the Constructive Equivalence
content: The theorem `tpc_iff_unbounded` proves that TPC is equivalent to the non-existence of a bound $M$ such that all twin prime lower elements are $\leq M$. Forward direction: given TPC, apply it to $M$ to obtain $p > M$ with $p$ a twin prime, contradicting the bound. Backward direction: apply `push_neg` to the negation `¬∃M, ∀p twin, p ≤ M` to get `∀M, ∃p twin, p > M`, which is exactly TPC with $N := M$.
mathContext:
$$	ext{TPC} \iff 
eg(\exists M : \mathbb{N},\  orall p : \mathbb{N},\ 	ext{IsTwinPrimePair}(p) \Rightarrow p \leq M)$$
The `push_neg` tactic converts $
eg\exists M,  orall p 	ext{ twin}, p \leq M$ to $ orall M, \exists p 	ext{ twin}, p > M$, which is TPC in disguise. The `omega` tactic closes the arithmetic gap $p > M \Rightarrow 
eg(p \leq M)$.

title: Unfolding TPC to the Explicit Simultaneous Primality Statement
content: `tpc_iff_prime_pairs` unfolds `IsTwinPrimePair` inside `TwinPrimeConjecture` to expose the raw simultaneous primality statement `∃ p > N, Nat.Prime p ∧ Nat.Prime (p+2)`. The proof is a single `simp only` with the definitional unfolding of `TwinPrimeConjecture` and `IsTwinPrimePair`. This form is useful when connecting TPC to Mathlib's `Nat.Prime` API without going through the `IsTwinPrimePair` wrapper.
mathContext:
$$\text{TPC} \iff \forall N : \mathbb{N},\ \exists p : \mathbb{N},\ p > N \wedge \text{Nat.Prime}(p) \wedge \text{Nat.Prime}(p+2)$$
This is the working form used in most papers on prime gaps. The equivalence is definitional: `IsTwinPrimePair p` is literally `Nat.Prime p ∧ Nat.Prime (p+2)` and `TwinPrimeConjecture` is the universal quantification over $N$.

title: 1-Line Proof: Axiom Instantly Gives Infinitely Many Twin Primes
content: `infinite_twin_prime_pairs` is a 1-line proof: `twin_prime_conjecture N`. This is the whole point of axiomatization — once TPC is declared as an axiom, every consequence that follows from TPC alone is a 1-line application of that axiom. The theorem is still meaningful: it names the consequence, gives it a discoverable type signature, and makes the logical dependency on `twin_prime_conjecture` explicit in the term structure. In a formal library, callers use `infinite_twin_prime_pairs` without even knowing that TPC is axiomatized — they just import and apply the theorem.
mathContext: The full proof term is `fun N => twin_prime_conjecture N`, where `twin_prime_conjecture : TwinPrimeConjecture = ∀ N, ∃ p > N, IsTwinPrimePair p`. This is a $\beta$-reduction: the axiom is exactly the statement being named. No computation, no simplification. The formalization value lies in the packaging: it wraps the axiom under a stable theorem name that clients can use without depending on implementation details of the axiom.

title: Conditional: Infinite Primes ≡ 5 (mod 6) via max(N, 3) Trick
content: `infinite_twin_primes_mod_six` is the most interesting conditional theorem. It needs `twin_prime_mod_six` which requires `p > 3`. The trick is to apply TPC at `max N 3` rather than `N`, getting a twin prime `p > max(N, 3)`. Then `Nat.le_max_left` and `Nat.le_max_right` extract both `p > N` and `p > 3` as corollaries, enabling the application of the structure theorem.
mathContext:
Proof structure: apply $\text{TPC}(\max(N,3))$ to obtain $p > \max(N,3)$ with $\text{IsTwinPrimePair}(p)$. Then:
- $p > N$ from $p > \max(N,3) \geq N$ (via `Nat.le_max_left`)
- $p > 3$ from $p > \max(N,3) \geq 3$ (via `Nat.le_max_right`)
- $p \equiv 5 \pmod{6}$ from `twin_prime_mod_six` applied to $p > 3$

Combined: TPC implies $\{p : \text{prime}, p \equiv 5 \pmod{6}\}$ is infinite.

title: No Finite Cover via Finset.sup Upper Bound
content: `no_finite_cover` shows every finite set `S : Finset ℕ` misses some twin prime. The key idea: apply TPC at `S.sup id` (the maximum element of `S`) to get a twin prime `p > S.sup id`. If `p ∈ S`, then `Finset.le_sup (f := id) hp_mem` gives `p ≤ S.sup id`, contradicting `p > S.sup id` via `omega`.
mathContext:
For a finite set $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, $\sup_{x \in S} x$ is the maximum element. TPC gives a twin prime $p > \sup S$. If $p \in S$ then $p \leq \sup S$ by definition of supremum — contradiction. The `Finset.le_sup (f := id) hp_mem` lemma applies because `S.sup id = S.sup (fun x => x)` is exactly the maximum.

This is a cleaner formulation of infinitude than `Set.Infinite` since it avoids infinite set machinery.
